narrative:
The model estimated a 56.6% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is only slightly above a coin flip, but it crossed the threshold used for this review, so your application was denied. This reflects a predicted risk of bar-exam failure, not a judgment that you cannot succeed.

The strongest factor driving the denial was your third-year class-standing decile. You were in decile 2, well below the average of about 5.8 among admitted students, and this was the largest push toward predicting failure. The second most important factor was your undergraduate GPA of 3.30, slightly above the admitted-student average of 3.23; this modestly pushed toward passing but did not outweigh your third-year standing. The third factor was your upper-middle family-income bracket, which added a smaller push toward failure; upper-middle income is common among admitted students at 45.4%, so this was not decisive on its own.

To address this, focus on controllable evidence of readiness: consider additional advanced coursework or a post-baccalaureate record, prepare to retake the LSAT, since your 34 is below the admitted average of about 37.2, and submit an addendum explaining your third-year performance and any improvement since. Seek admissions advising about schools and support programs that consider bar-passage risk holistically. Gender and race were not used.
